answer:
RESULT — median wealth in 1985 among the ever-incarcerated (ever_jailed = 1, n = 289 of 12,013; 2.41%). Outcome = composite_wealth_1985 in nominal 1985 dollars; zeros (no assets) and negatives (net debt) retained; 1,899 duplicate rows retained. CI = percentile bootstrap of the median (B=2,000; B=4,000 for shares; seed 20261022). All numbers below come from the executed scripts.

PRIMARY TABLE (ever-incarcerated only; reference column at the end)
group | n | q25 | median | 95% CI | q75 | p90 | IQR | share ≤ $0
ALL | 289 | 0 | $720 | [0, 1,200] | 6,000 | 17,300 | 6,000 | 45.0% [39.1, 50.5]
race black | 159 | 0 | $320 | [0, 1,060] | 4,700 | 15,896 | 4,700 | 47.8% [39.6, 55.3]
race hispanic | 61 | 0 | $0 (literally zero) | [0, 1,560] | 5,500 | 9,690 | 5,500 | 52.5% [39.3, 63.9]
race white | 69 | 0 | $2,200 | [400, 5,200] | 9,100 | 30,000 | 9,100 | 31.9% [20.3, 43.5]
sex male | 252 | 0 | $1,000 | [300, 1,480] | 6,258 | 17,170 | 6,258 | 41.3% [35.3, 47.2]
sex female | 37 | 0 | $0 (literally zero) | [0, 0] degenerate | 3,100 | 13,040 | 3,100 | 70.3% [56.7, 83.8]
black male | 143 | 0 | $800 | [0, 1,400] | 5,900 | 15,974 | 5,900 | 44.1%
hispanic male | 52 | 0 | $700 | [0, 3,000] | 6,000 | 9,892 | 6,000 | 46.2%
white male | 57 | 0 | $2,000 | [400, 5,200] | 9,100 | 25,600 | 9,100 | 29.8%
black female | 16 | 0 | $0 | [0,0] | 0 | 2,550 | 0 | 81.2% — n<30, shown, NOT interpreted
hispanic female | 9 | 0 | $0 | [0,0] | 0 | 1,280 | 0 | 88.9% — n<30, shown, NOT interpreted
white female | 12 | 0 | $4,100 | [0, 20,700] | 14,050 | 45,430 | 14,050 | 41.7% — n<30, shown, NOT interpreted
REFERENCE (never incarcerated, all) | 11,724 | 0 | $3,600 | [3,300, 3,900] | 16,100 | 66,910 | 16,100 | 31.8%

NAMED RESULT 1 — the male race contrast (the only cell block with adequate n): white men $2,000 vs black men $800 (difference +$1,200, bootstrap CI [−600, +4,800], permutation p = 0.12) vs hispanic men $700 (+$1,300, CI [−1,400, +4,800], p = 0.29); black vs hispanic men are indistinguishable ($800 vs $700, p = 0.87). Asset poverty in the same cells: white men 29.8%, black men 44.1%, hispanic men 46.2%. So among incarcerated men the level ordering is white > (black ≈ hispanic), and it is not statistically secure at n=252.

NAMED RESULT 2 — pooled male vs female: median $1,000 vs $0 (+$1,000, bootstrap CI [+300, +1,480], permutation p = 0.18), and asset poverty 41.3% vs 70.3% (CI [56.7, 83.8]). The female median is exactly $0 with a degenerate CI because >64.9% of the 37 ever-incarcerated women have exactly zero wealth; I report it literally rather than substituting the female mean ($7,516).

FIRST-CLASS RESULT — asset poverty (share at zero or below) is the most stable disparity signal, as you anticipated: ever-incarcerated overall 45.0% vs 31.8% never-incarcerated; hispanic 52.5% / black 47.8% / white 31.9%; female 70.3% / male 41.3%. Its CIs are narrow relative to the median CIs, because 39.4% of the 289 sit on an exact $0 tie, which makes median CIs collapse toward zero.

QUANTILE LADDER — is the racial gap at the bottom or the top? At the top, in dollars. q10 and q25 are $0 for all three races (the bottom is compressed by ties at zero, so nothing can be measured there); median black−white = −$1,880; q75 = −$4,400; p90 = −$14,104. As ratios the pattern inverts: black/white = 0.15x at the median, 0.52x at q75, 0.53x at p90. Read plainly: the racial gap in this subsample is a level shift at the bottom (a higher share of black and hispanic respondents have nothing at all) and a widening dollar gap at the top (white respondents reach $30,000 at p90 and $244,600 max, vs $15,896/$136,573 for black and $9,690/$85,000 for hispanic); among those with positive wealth the medians nearly converge ($4,400 black, $6,000 hispanic, $6,000 white).

RACE vs SEX — which is larger, and what the data will not support. Race shows the larger spread of group medians (white $2,200 − hispanic $0 = $2,200, plus $14,104 at p90 and a 20.6-point asset-poverty gap white vs hispanic) than sex ($1,000 at the median, 29-point asset-poverty gap but at n=37). Rank-based variation is small and identical for both cuts (Kruskal-Wallis: race H=5.32 p=0.070; sex H=5.12 p=0.024; rank eta² = 0.017 for both) — i.e. each cut explains ~2% of variation, so the disparities are real in the sense of consistent ordering but weak in magnitude, and neither cut dominates. The data will NOT support: (i) race-specific conclusions for women (n=9/12/16; the $4,100 white-female median has a CI of [0, $20,700] and is an artefact of a 12-person cell), (ii) any race x sex interaction claim, (iii) any statement about the bottom of the distribution given q10=q25=$0 ties. Note a statistical tension I am flagging rather than hiding: the permutation test on the white−black median difference gives p=0.010 while the bootstrap CI [−127, +4,950] includes zero — a known instability when a large mass sits at exactly zero; I therefore describe the racial gap as suggestive, not established.

REFERENCE COLUMN ONLY (context, not the story): ever-incarcerated median $720 vs $3,600 never-incarcerated (−$2,880, ratio 0.20x). Cell-wise, the shortfall is largest for hispanic ($0 vs $3,400; ratio undefined) and white ($2,200 vs $5,700, 0.39x) and smallest for black ($320 vs $764, 0.42x) — because never-incarcerated black respondents were already near $0 in 1985 (median $764, 43.4% at or below zero).

NOMINAL TREND (robustness only, not deflated; cross-year comparisons mix real change with inflation): among the ever-incarcerated the median falls $720 (1985) → $0 (1990) → $0 (1996) and asset poverty rises 45.0% → 56.7% → 63.0%, vs never-incarcerated $10,500 (1990) and $8,500 (1996), 29.2% / 40.4%. The disparity widens over the window in every race group.

PLAIN-LANGUAGE STATEMENT (bounded by n=289): Among NLSY79 respondents ever jailed between 1985 and 1994, 1985 wealth was essentially nil — median $720, with 45% holding zero or negative assets. Within this group the sharpest line is race: ever-incarcerated white respondents held about three to seven times the median wealth of black respondents ($2,200 vs $320) and strictly more than hispanic respondents (whose median is exactly $0), and 31.9% of white vs 47.8% of black and 52.5% of hispanic respondents had nothing or debt. Sex cuts the other way at the bottom: ever-incarcerated women were far more likely to have nothing at all (70.3% vs 41.3% of men), giving a median of exactly $0 against men's $1,000. Because every group's lower quartile is $0, the racial gap is invisible at the bottom and shows up in dollars only above the median, widest at the 90th percentile. These are descriptive within-sample disparities, not effects of incarceration.

LIMITATIONS CARRIED INTO THE WRITE-UP (as agreed): (1) Timing mismatch — ever_jailed covers jail 1985–1994 while wealth is measured in 1985, so most incarceration spells post-date the outcome; the comparison is a baseline disparity among people who later/became incarcerated, subject to selection and reverse causation (low wealth raising incarceration risk), and any 1985 spell could mechanically depress 1985 wealth; no causal reading is offered. (2) ever_jailed is unverifiable here — the file contains only the six columns and no place-of-residence or detention-facility field, so the flag could not be cross-validated against a "Jail" residence record; jail cannot be separated from prison, nor short from long spells. (3) Small cells — n<30 female race cells shown but excluded from interpretation; female results rest on n=37. (4) Generalisation — no sampling weights, household survey frame that omits people incarcerated in 1985 and likely under-represents zero-wealth non-contacts, so results describe this NLSY79 sample only. (5) Data quality — 1,899 duplicate rows retained because no respondent ID makes de-duplication auditable; values rounded to $100 in 81% of rows.

payload.hypothesis: Among the 289 NLSY79 respondents ever incarcerated (jailed 1985-1994), 1985 wealth was essentially nil - median $720 (95% bootstrap CI $0-$1,200) with 45.0% holding zero or negative assets - and the disparities within this group run mainly along race, with a second, bottom-of-the-distribution divide along sex. Median 1985 wealth was $2,200 for ever-incarcerated white respondents, $320 for black respondents, and exactly $0 for hispanic respondents (asset poverty 31.9%, 47.8% and 52.5% respectively); the white-black gap is +$1,880 (permutation p=0.010 but bootstrap CI -127 to +$4,950, so suggestive rather than established) and the black-hispanic difference is negligible ($320, p=0.79). Among men, the only adequately powered race contrast, white men ($2,000, 29.8% at or below zero) held roughly 2.5 times the median wealth of black men ($800, 44.1%) and hispanic men ($700, 46.2%), though neither difference is statistically secure at n=252. The ever-incarcerated female median is literally $0 (n=37; CI degenerate because 64.9% have exactly zero wealth) versus $1,000 for men, and the female-male asset-poverty gap (70.3% vs 41.3%) is the more stable signal than the median gap itself. Race-specific results for women (n=16, 9, 12) are reported but not interpretable, and no race x sex interaction can be supported. Because q10 and q25 are $0 in every race group, the racial gap is invisible at the bottom and appears only as a level shift in the share with nothing, widening in dollars above the median (median -$1,880, q75 -$4,400, p90 -$14,104 for black vs white) while positive-wealth medians nearly converge ($4,400 vs $6,000). Race accounts for somewhat more spread than sex (median range $2,200 vs $1,000; both cuts explain only ~2% of rank variation, Kruskal-Wallis p=0.07 and p=0.02). These are descriptive, within-sample disparities measured at the start of the 1985-1994 incarceration window, so they characterise the wealth profile of people who are incarcerated during the window rather than an effect of incarceration; the flag cannot be cross-validated (no place-of-residence or detention-facility field exists in this file), jail cannot be distinguished from prison or short from long spells, and with no sampling weights and a household survey frame the results do not generalise beyond this NLSY79 sample.
payload.workflow: Read data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; 6 columns); relabelled 'hipanic'->'hispanic'; retained all zeros/negatives and the 1,899 duplicate rows; defined the primary population as ever_jailed==1 (n=289) and the never-incarcerated (n=11,724) as reference only. For the primary population computed, overall and by race, sex and race x sex: n, q25, median, q75, p90, IQR, mean, min/max, share with wealth <=0 / ==0 / <0 / >0, and percentile-bootstrap 95% CIs for medians (B=2,000) and for asset-poverty shares (B=4,000; seed 20261022). Added medians restricted to strictly positive wealth, dollar differences and ratios vs the never-incarcerated group in the same demographic cell (ratios only where both medians >0), a q10-q25-median-q75-p90 ladder by race to locate the gap in the distribution, Kruskal-Wallis and rank eta-squared to compare the race and sex cuts, B=20,000 permutation tests for median differences, Mann-Whitney male-only race contrasts, threshold tail shares ($0/$1k/$10k/$50k/$100k), and a clearly-labelled nominal-dollar 1990/1996 trend as robustness only. Applied the agreed thresholds (n>=30 headline; 20-29 indicative, unstable; n<30 shown with n and CIs but excluded from race-specific female conclusions).
